input.raw_text: Halfway through 2023 and the soft-landing trade has become consensus almost without anyone noticing the handoff. June CPI printed at three percent, inflation is clearly rolling over, and the Fed still hiked last week to five-and-a-quarter — likely the last one, everyone now says. The S&P closed out July around 4,590, the best first half since 2019, yet the leadership is startlingly narrow: Nvidia's blowout guidance lit the AI fuse, and Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Tesla have done the real lifting while the equal-weight index badly lags. Advance-decline lines are weak, most stocks never participated, and strategists keep abandoning recession calls — jobless claims won't cooperate, banks passed their stress tests, and consumers keep spending. Ten-year Treasury is near four percent, credit spreads have tightened all year. I'm suspicious of a market where a handful of stocks are the trade, but fighting the tape has been expensive.
input.summary: By the end of July 2023, falling inflation and resilient economic data had made a soft landing increasingly consensual despite the Federal Reserve's latest rate increase. The S&P 500 showed strong momentum, but gains were concentrated in a small group of technology-oriented mega-cap companies while equal-weight performance and advance-decline measures remained weak. Recession expectations were receding as labor conditions, bank stress tests, and consumer spending stayed resilient; meanwhile, the ten-year Treasury yield was near four percent and credit spreads had narrowed. The combination of persistent equity strength and unusually narrow participation remained a source of concern and uncertainty.
